title: Fat Rascals
subtitle: Yorkshire fruit scones with a crisp orange-flavoured crust
excerpt: Fat rascals are a Yorkshire speciality: large, round fruit scones enriched with mixed peel and spice, decorated with cherries and almonds before baking. The crust goes crisp while the interior stays soft. Makes 8.
sourceNotes: Fat rascals are a regional Yorkshire bake, most closely associated with Bettys Cafe Tea Rooms in Harrogate and York, where they have been sold since the 1980s in the form that most people now recognise: round, thick, and decorated with two glacé cherry eyes and almond 'teeth'. The name appears in older Yorkshire recipe collections as a variant of teacake or spiced scone. The earlier versions were plainer and less theatrical in appearance. The decorative face with cherries and almonds was introduced by Bettys but has now become synonymous with the name in commercial contexts; the home version is equally valid without the face.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze baked fat rascals, wrapped individually. Warm in a low oven from frozen.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Best eaten the day they are made.

glossaryTerms.definition: Working cold fat into flour with the fingertips until the mixture resembles breadcrumbs. Keep the butter cold and work quickly to avoid melting it; the pockets of fat are what create a flaky, tender texture in the final bake.

content.text: Fat rascals are somewhere between a scone and a rock cake: thicker and richer than a scone, with a crisper outer crust, but not as dry and compact as a rock cake. The fruit inside is studded with mixed peel and plumped currants. Orange zest in the dough gives them a clean citrus note that cuts through the richness.

cold butter into flour, then mixing in fruit and liquid. It should hold together without being sticky. Shape into thick rounds by hand; they do not need to be perfectly smooth. Glaze with egg before baking, and if you want the traditional face, press two glacé cherries and a few blanched almonds into the surface before they go into the oven.
Heat the oven to 190°C fan (210°C conventional). Line a large baking tray with baking parchment.

Put {{plain-flour}} of plain flour, {{baking-powder}} of baking powder, {{cinnamon-ground}} of ground cinnamon, and {{mixed-spice}} of mixed spice into a bowl. Add {{unsalted-butter}} of cold cubed butter (and lard if using) and rub in with fingertips until the mixture looks like coarse breadcrumbs. Stir in {{caster-sugar}} of caster sugar.

Add {{currants}} of currants, {{mixed-peel}} of mixed peel, and the orange zest. Beat the egg with {{whole-milk}} of milk and pour into the dry ingredients. Stir until the dough just comes together. It should hold its shape without being sticky.
Divide into 8 pieces and shape each into a round about 7 cm across and 2 cm thick. Place on the lined tray, spaced apart. Brush with beaten egg.

If decorating, press two glacé cherries and three blanched almonds into each round in the traditional face pattern. Bake for 18 to 20 minutes until deep golden brown. Cool slightly on the tray before eating.

items.symptom: Fat rascals spread flat in the oven
items.cause: Dough too soft, or butter too warm
items.fix: Keep the butter cold. If the dough feels sticky, refrigerate for 15 minutes before shaping.

items.symptom: Inside is still doughy when the crust is brown
items.fix: Keep each round to 2 cm in height. Thicker rounds need lower temperature and longer time: 170°C fan for 25 to 28 minutes.

content.text: Fat rascals are a Yorkshire thing. Outside the county they are largely unknown. Within it, particularly in Harrogate and York, they are associated with afternoon tea and the distinctive teatime culture of the county. The decorated version with cherry eyes is theatrical in a way that most British bakes are not, which may explain why they have acquired a certain reputation. At home they are simpler and just as good: a thick, crisp-crusted, fragrant bun that pairs well with strong Yorkshire tea.
